22485.etyen:
Inherited from Middle Norwegian harfr (“harrow”). The formally corresponding Old Norse harfr is attested as a byname; compare the ordinary Old Norse common noun herfi (“harrow”).
Kroonen reconstructs Proto-Germanic *harbō- behind Bokmål harv and Nynorsk horv, alongside a variant *harbja- behind Icelandic herfi (“harrow”). These are probably related to Proto-Germanic *harbistaz (“autumn, harvest season”) and an inferred verb *harbijaną (“to pluck”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kerp- (“to pluck, pick; reap, harvest”). The deeper connection is not entirely certain.
Compare Norwegian Nyno

1000149.etyen:
PIE word
 *bʰardʰéh₂
Inherited from Old Norse Svalbarð, officially adopted as the Norwegian name of the archipelago in 1925. Before then, Spitsbergen was used for both the archipelago and its largest island.
The medieval name is recorded in Icelandic annals under the year 1194 in forms such as Svalbarðs fundr (“discovery of Svalbard”) and Svalbarði fundinn (“Svalbard found”). Landnámabók likewise mentions Svalbarði, describing it as lying several days' sailing north of Langanes in Iceland. It is uncertain whether the land referred to in these medieval sources was any part of the modern Svalbar

1000405.etyen:
Derived from Latin Antarctica, a New Latin geographical name from Ancient Greek ἀνταρκτικός (antarktikós, “opposite the Arctic; southern”), from ἀντ- (ant-, “opposite, against”) + ἀρκτικός (arktikós, “Arctic, northern”). The second element is ultimately from ἄρκτος (árktos, “bear; the Great Bear”), referring to the northern constellations. The name therefore literally denotes the region opposite the Arctic. Doublet of Antarktika (“Antarctica, specifically the continent”)
Compare Danish Antarktis, Swedish Antarktis, German Antarktis, Dutch Antarctica and English Antarctica.

1002453.etyen:
PIE word
 *h₂epó
Compound of a priori (“a priori”) + -isme (“-ism”).
The base, a priori (“a priori”), is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“from the former; from first principles”), literally “from the former”.
The first element, ā (“from”), is a form of ab (“from, away from”), inherited from Proto-Italic *ap (“from, away from”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”).
The second element, priōrī, is the ablative singular of prior (“earlier, former, previous”), from Proto-Italic *priōs (“earlier, previous”), from earlier Proto-Italic *prijōs, from *pri (“before”) and *-jō

1005013.etyen:
First attested in the by 1900.
Compound of skog (“forest”) + bestand (“stand, stock”), literally “forest stand”.
The first part skog (“forest”) is inherited from Old Norse skógr (“forest, wood”), from Proto-Germanic *skōgaz (“forest, wood”), of uncertain further origin. The last part bestand (“stand, stock”) is from Middle Low German bestant (“stock, quantity; continuance”), a verbal noun of bestān (“to remain, stand”), ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *stāną (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”).
